summary.text: A tsunami is a series of waves set off when a large volume of water is suddenly pushed out of place, usually in an ocean or a large lake.
Earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, landslides, glacier calvings and meteorite impacts can all start one, unlike ordinary waves raised by wind or tides pulled by the Moon and Sun.
Its wavelength is far longer than a normal wave's, so it may first look like a rapidly rising tide rather than a breaking wave, yet it can affect entire ocean basins.

facts.label: Gap between waves
facts.value: Minutes to hours, arriving as a wave train

facts.label: 2004 Indian Ocean toll
facts.value: At least 230,000 killed or missing in 14 countries

facts.label: Early explanation
facts.value: Thucydides tied them to undersea earthquakes

items.prompt: At the beach, you notice the sea climbing quickly up the sand like a tide coming in far too fast, with no big curling crest. What could this be?

options.label: An ordinary high tide arriving on schedule
A wind-driven storm wave about to break
The first sign of an arriving tsunami
A rip current pulling water out to sea

items.explain: Instead of breaking like a surf wave, a tsunami may at first look like a very fast rising tide.

items.prompt: Why do scientists avoid calling tsunamis 'tidal waves'?

options.label: Tides come from the Moon and Sun, but tsunamis come from displaced water
Tsunamis are too small and slow to count as real waves
Tsunamis only ever strike coasts at the moment of low tide
The Japanese word is the only name allowed by international law

items.explain: The name suggests tides cause tsunamis, but tides come from the gravity of the Moon and Sun while tsunamis come from large displacements of water.

items.prompt: A huge section of a glacier breaks off and crashes into the sea. Could this set off a tsunami?

options.label: No, only earthquakes under the sea floor can do that
No, unless a strong wind is blowing at the same time
Only if it happens exactly at high tide
Yes, because it suddenly displaces a large volume of water

items.explain: Any large disturbance that displaces enough water, including glacier calving, can generate a tsunami.

items.prompt: A tsunami's first wave floods a seaside town and then drains away. Is it safe to go back down to the shore?

options.label: Yes, a tsunami is a single wave that is now spent
No, more waves may follow minutes or hours later
Yes, as long as the water level looks normal again
No, but only because of strong wind waves afterwards

items.explain: Tsunamis usually arrive as a wave train, a series of waves with periods from minutes to hours.

items.prompt: The word 'tsunami' was borrowed from Japanese. What does it literally mean?

options.label: Great wave
Earthquake water
Angry sea
Harbour wave

items.explain: The Japanese word means 'harbour wave', even though the waves do not only strike harbours.

items.prompt: Roughly how many people were killed or went missing in the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami?

options.label: About 2,300
About 23,000
At least 230,000
Over 2 million

items.explain: At least 230,000 people were killed or missing across 14 countries bordering the Indian Ocean.
